questions.question: Why is the output rate about 4x the input rate on the example bills?
options: Input tokens are processed in one parallel prefill pass, while output tokens must be generated serially, one full forward pass each
Output tokens crowd the context window far more than input tokens
A call usually produces far more output tokens than input tokens
Vendors subsidize input pricing to attract longer prompts
questions.explanation: See the "The billing formula: two lines of arithmetic" section: input tokens are processed in one parallel prefill pass, while output tokens must be generated serially, one full forward pass each.

questions.question: Plan B has more input tokens than Plan A (1500 vs 900), yet its per-call cost drops from about ¥0.0292 to about ¥0.0132. Why?
options: Plan B switched to a cheaper model
Plan B's longer input hit the prompt cache
The longer input triggered a tiered-pricing discount
The format declaration cut output from 1600 to 450 tokens, and those savings far outweigh the extra input — the direct corollary of output costing 4x
questions.explanation: See the "The arithmetic of three bills" section: the format declaration costs a few hundred extra input tokens, yet the output savings far outweigh them — the direct corollary of "output costs 4×".

questions.question: In day-to-day engineering, which cost lever ranks first by value?
options: Caching: fix the stable, unchanging prefix byte for byte so hits bill at a deep discount
Deleting redundant background from the system prompt
questions.explanation: See the "Ranking the levers, and model differences" section: first comes caching — hits bill at a deep discount and the hit rate decides the savings, while switching models is the last card to play.
